name: Desoxymethyltestosterone (DMT / Madol)

lead: Desoxymethyltestosterone is an oral anabolic steroid invented in 1961 and shelved. It resurfaced in 2005 when it was supplied to the BALCO operation and was later found in bodybuilding supplements.
All evidence about its effects comes from rat and cell studies; there are no clinical trials.

paras: It is a modified form of DHT that activates the androgen receptor and increased muscle mass in castrated rats with little effect on prostate weight.

Animal studies at higher doses reported liver damage and heart enlargement. It is a Schedule III controlled substance in the US, Class C in the UK, and prohibited in sport. Supplements labelled with it have sometimes contained other compounds.

lead: Desoxymethyltestosterone (DMT, also called Madol and sold under names such as Pheraplex) is a synthetic, orally active anabolic-androgenic steroid, a 17α-methyl derivative of dihydrotestosterone (DHT) that lacks the usual 3-keto group [1]. It is unrelated to the hallucinogen dimethyltryptamine, which shares the abbreviation [1].

It was invented by Max Huffman in 1961 and described in 1963, but never marketed as a drug [1]. It re-emerged in 2005, when chemist Patrick Arnold produced it and supplied it to Victor Conte of BALCO; it was identified as a doping agent and found in over-the-counter bodybuilding supplements [1][2].

Rat studies indicate substantial anabolic activity, and in vitro tests found it activates the androgen receptor; no clinical trials of it exist [1][3]. It is a US Schedule III controlled substance and prohibited in sport [2][4].

paras: The compound was patented by Huffman in 1961 and described in the literature in 1963 but not developed commercially [1]. In 2005 Patrick Arnold rediscovered it and supplied it to BALCO, and it drew attention after being detected as a doping agent and in bodybuilding supplements [1][3]. It was among the early designer steroids marketed to athletes and bodybuilders [1].

A 2007 study synthesised DMT and characterised its profile: in cell assays its ability to activate androgen-receptor-dependent gene expression was substantial, and it also had anabolic effects in rats [3]. Wikipedia reports rat data of about 160% anabolic and 60% androgenic activity relative to testosterone, a 6.5:1 ratio, and androgen receptor binding about half that of DHT [1]. In castrated rats it increased levator ani muscle weight without changing prostate or seminal vesicle weights [1], and a 2011 rat study found it shifted muscle myosin heavy chain expression in a pattern similar to testosterone [5].
Metabolism studies have characterised urinary metabolites to improve doping detection [6][7].

Adverse effects in people have not been systematically studied. Animal studies at higher doses reported liver damage and left ventricular hypertrophy, typical of 17α-alkylated steroids [1]. A 2008 laboratory study found DMT and 19-norandrostenedione induced micronuclei in cultured hamster cells, an indicator of potential genotoxicity [8]. A 2016 case report described drug-induced liver injury in two deployed US service members who used prohormone supplements containing anabolic-androgenic steroids [9].

Analysts found DMT or its prodrug 17α-methylepithiostanol in products sold as dietary supplements such as Epistane and P-Plex [2]. A 2025 analysis of a capsule labelled as DMT found it contained a different compound [10]. DMT is prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency [2].

DMT became a Schedule III anabolic steroid in the US on 4 January 2010 [1]; a 2009 final rule in the Federal Register classified three steroids under the Controlled Substances Act [4]. In the UK it is Class C [1].
No studies found of clinical use in people. Evidence is limited to animal, cell and analytical studies [3][5][8], plus a case report of liver injury from steroid-containing supplements [9].
